title: Litter in a Clean or Dirty Garage
text:
In 1990 Robert Cialdini, Raymond Reno and Carl Kallgren published a series of experiments on why people litter. In one, people returning to their cars in a parking garage found a large handbill tucked under the windshield wiper. The researchers watched whether they threw it on the ground.

The garage had been arranged in advance. Sometimes it was spotless; sometimes it was strewn with handbills, cigarette butts and candy wrappers. And as each person walked toward their car, a passing research assistant either simply walked by or dropped a handbill on the ground in plain view.

People littered more in the dirty garage than in the clean one: litter signaled that littering was what people did there. But the assistant's action changed things in an interesting way. In the dirty garage, seeing someone else litter drew attention to the mess and made people litter the most of all. In the clean garage, seeing someone drop a handbill made people litter the least, because the single piece of trash stood out as an exception against the clean floor.

Further studies showed that messages drawing attention to the norm, whether about what most people do or what most people approve of, could reduce littering, as long as people's attention was focused on the norm at the moment they acted.
lesson: People take cues from what others around them seem to do. Keep shared spaces in good order, and point out the good behavior that is common rather than the bad.
people: Robert Cialdini, Raymond Reno, Carl Kallgren
source: Cialdini, R. B., Reno, R. R., and Kallgren, C. A. (1990). A focus theory of normative conduct: Recycling the concept of norms to reduce littering in public places. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 58(6), 1015-1026.
